16578-the-kipling-reader-selections-from:
Macmillan's Kipling Reader, new and revised edition of 1923, gathers the author's best prose and poetry for schools and general readers. Prose leads with Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, William the Conqueror, Wee Willie Winkie, Mowgli's Brothers, and Tiger Tiger. Poetry follows with The Native Born, The Flowers, The English Flag, and The Overland Mail.

First issued in 1900 and reprinted many times, the reader proved its lasting appeal. The selections span India, the jungle, and England, in Kipling's vigorous style. Readers new to Kipling will find a strong single-volume introduction to his world.
16598-history-of-the-american-negro-in-t:
W. Allison Sweeney, contributing editor of the Chicago Defender, records Black American service in the Great War in this illustrated 1919 history. The book also resumes past service: the Revolution, 1812, the Rebellion, frontier Indian wars, the Spanish-American War, and Mexico. Official War Department records back the account, with tributes from French and American commanders.

A full summary of the 370th, the Old Eighth, anchors the volume. Sweeney writes with pride and documentary care, naming units, battles, and honors. The book stands as an early, essential record of Black soldiers' splendid service in Europe.
18997-the-vicomte-de-bragelonne-or-ten-y:
Alexandre Dumas wrote this long romance as the completion of The Three Musketeers and Twenty Years After. This copy is volume four of part two in a nine-volume 1893 edition, richly drawn with pen and wood cuts. It carries the court of Louis the Fourteenth into fresh intrigue.

Louise de la Valliere pleads with the king, Saint-Aignan spies from behind tapestry, and old musketeer ties strain under love and ambition. Court manners hide sharp power plays at every turn. Readers get grand, crowded historical romance, where honour, passion, and royal favour decide fates.
22733-socialism-a-summary-and-interpreta:
John Spargo wrote Socialism: A Summary and Interpretation of Socialist Principles, a clear-headed handbook of socialist thought for general readers. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Spargo, an English-born American writer, aimed to state what socialism actually claimed, against the caricatures that filled newspapers.

Both of the old crude views, he writes, are now happily well-nigh extinct. Misconception of socialism's meaning remains widespread, and the ignorance shown on every hand is often disheartening, but the puerile misrepresentations are no longer met in serious discussion. From that clearing of ground, the book builds its summary of doctrine. It served as a standard introduction for a generation, and it still shows how the movement explained itself in its strongest American years.
31807-the-plague-at-marseilles-consider-:
Richard Bradley's 1721 treatise, in its third edition, considers the plague at Marseilles and adds remarks on plague in general, its cause and nature of infection, and precautions to prevent its spread. Dedicated to Sir Isaac Newton, president of the Royal Society, it was published for the preservation of the people of Great Britain.

Bradley draws on physicians who resided at infected places. One physician at Aix reports carbuncles, buboes, livid blisters, and purple spots, with more than fifty deaths a day for three weeks. Readers get an early eighteenth-century medical work, urgent and practical, written while pestilence raged in the south of France.
9670-specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-:
Volume one of George Gilfillan's Specimens, with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets, opens with an essay on the origin of English poetry. Gilfillan traces verse from Roman Britain through a glimmering dawn to Chaucer, father of English poetry, and Gower. He notes that Rome left Britain nearly as rude as it found it, with no British-born Latin masters. The essay then follows Arthur's coronation spouts and solemnities.

Later pages in the volume pair early poets with memoirs and choice pieces. Gilfillan writes as a guide, not a pedant, for general readers. A reader gets a learned yet readable start to English verse, and a sense of how poetry grew from chronicle to art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tepl:
Tepl is a Premonstratensian abbey in western Bohemia, in the Archdiocese of Prague. The blessed martyr Hroznata, a Bohemian nobleman, founded it in 1193. Its first monks came from Strahov Abbey in Prague. Tepl escaped damage in the Hussite Wars, through Abbot Racko's military spirit and his relatives' aid. It suffered more in the Reformation, when Luther's doctrine won abbey subjects. A rebellion rose in 1525 and ended only with the ringleaders' execution.

In following years monks left the order and married. Abbot Johann Kurz restored discipline and founded a theological school. His successor Meyskönig, with the archbishop's aid, improved monastery and school. He brought subjects back to the Church by compulsion. Andreas Ebersbach raised the abbey until it was called the nursery of pastoral work. It serves twenty-four parishes, runs a school and the Pilsen gymnasium, owns the Marienbad cure, and supports hospitals at both places.
doe-osti-2569883-machine-learning-for-re:
A final report by David R. Smith of the University of Wisconsin covers machine learning for real-time prediction and control of fusion plasma behavior. The test bed is DIII-D, a tokamak where sudden edge bursts called ELMs can damage the machine. The project built deep neural networks that read beam emission spectroscopy, a fluctuation diagnostic, and flag events early enough for the plasma control system to react.

Models were shaped for fast chips such as FPGAs, using a data-flow design fed by 64 channels sampled at one megahertz. One model predicts time to the next type-I ELM from a 128 microsecond window of data. It performed best around an eight millisecond horizon, about what DIII-D needs to fire suppression coils in time. Training ran on the Perlmutter supercomputer. The team judges the approach feasible, while stating plainly that a reliable predictor needs more work.
doe-osti-2583947-grid-interactive-micro-:
Final report for award DE-EE0009684 was submitted by Copeland of Sidney, Ohio, with Suresh Shivashankar as lead investigator, covering October 2021 to March 2025. The product is a supermarket staple reimagined: a self-contained, chilled open display case with thermal storage built in. Open cases spill cold air into aisles all day. This design set out to waste far less of it, and to shift when the case draws power.

Four targets framed the work. The case should save thirty percent of the energy current open cases use. It should cut peak demand eighty percent over two hours by discharging stored cold. It should spill at least half as much chilled air, and pay back within three years under time-of-use pricing. Albertsons advised on food safety, ComEd on utility incentives, and case maker Arneg on production. Three phases moved from design through construction to full system testing.
doe-osti-3013971-time-space-and-molecule:
Chuji Wang of Mississippi State University submitted this final report for grant DE-SC0021530, covering January 2021 to December 2023, on measuring plasma reactive species with cavity ringdown spectroscopy. Low-temperature plasmas make reactive molecules such as hydroxyl and nitric oxide that drive applications from medicine to water treatment. Measuring them at a water surface, or under it, defeats most instruments.

Wang's group built a Brewster angle cavity ringdown system and aimed it at three zones: the plasma gas, the water surface, and below the surface. A stable helium plasma jet ran at a low flow of 315 standard cubic centimeters per minute without visibly disturbing the liquid. The project trained two graduate students, one of whom finished a PhD in December 2022 and joined ASML as a processing engineer.
doe-osti-3017346-direct-ink-write-and-pr:
Laurie Jin, Bruce Yang, Beck Walton, Rick Hynes, and Xavier Mayali of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this February 2026 report on direct ink write printing with calcium carbonate slurries. Ocean acidification is cutting calcification in the sea, and coral reefs are losing the coral-algae partnership that sustains them. The team asked whether printed mineral structures could give that partnership a place to regrow.

They formulated a ceramic ink from a diacrylate polymer mixed with calcium carbonate, the material of coral skeletons. The slurry thins under shear, which is what makes it printable. Rheology tests confirmed the printing behavior. Printed parts showed strong control over feature size and infill design, and varied infill patterns were tried. Print beds moved at 10 to 20 millimeters per second depending on part complexity. Reef restoration teams get a candidate material for structures designed to grow algae in the ocean.
doe-osti-3017711-experimental-validation: Ben Dudson's hosted record is a single summary slide, LLNL-TR-2014923 from February 2026, for a paper accepted in Nuclear Fusion in 2026. It reports experimental validation of the Hermes-3 code, run inside the BOUT++ framework, for predictive simulation of the plasma boundary in magnetic fusion devices. Using only total power of 120 kilowatts, a particle flux figure, and the magnetic equilibrium as inputs, with no tuning parameters, Hermes-3 predicted plasma profiles and fluctuations. Agreement with the TCV-X21 experiment was better than the comparison cases the slide cites.
doe-osti-3364019-demonstration-of-algori:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-26/6, dated March 2026, demonstrates an algorithm that chooses where to place sensors inside a nuclear system. Authors Haoyu Wang, Roberto Ponciroli, and Richard B. Vilim of Argonne worked with Vasileios Theos, Jonah Lau, and Stylianos Chatzidakis of Purdue University. The method uses simulation data rather than a physical test rig. Neural networks first learn how disturbances spread through the system.

The placement step then picks detector spots whose responses reveal the most about hidden interior changes. A sensitivity matrix links each detector to the disturbance modes the network learned. Candidate locations on the boundary compete, and the chosen set maximizes information about the interior. Good placement means fewer sensors can still catch faults early. The demonstration shows the full pipeline running on simulated data.
doe-osti-3484554-specimen-sizing-and-rem:
Argonne report ANL-AMMT-029, by Bipul Barua, works out specimen sizing and remaining life samples for high temperature reactor material surveillance. Surveillance samples let operators judge how reactor metals age in service. Sample size and count must be set before parts go in.

The workflow pairs a spreadsheet with the MPC Omega method named in the text. Three workflow inconsistencies are named and shared by every sample problem. Their size impact is quantified once, then reported for a second problem. Creep-rate models differ inside the one workflow, one flagged clash. Engineers get life estimates with known weak spots marked.
history-of-the-american-negro-in-the-gre:
W Allison Sweeney, a contributing editor of the Chicago Defender, wrote this history in 1919. Its long title promises the splendid record of Black troops in Europe's battle zones. Sweeney adds a resume of past service, from the Revolution to Mexico. War Department records and commanders' tributes back the account, he states.

One French citation tells of a commander who held a hard sector under shelling. The same officer led a battalion across the Ailette canal and won the Croix de Guerre. Portraits and named tributes fill the book. Sweeney wrote to fix a record he feared white historians would slight.
nasa-tm-19650003005-environmental-testin:
W D Hoggard II, test and evaluation support manager for the project, wrote this final report at Goddard on October 6, 1964. It covers ground testing of the Ionosphere Explorer spacecraft before launch. The craft was built to study the ionosphere, the charged upper layer of the air.

Hoggard records the test history through to launch, along with telemetry data. Ground tests expose a spacecraft to harsh conditions before flight does. A final report like this one lets later teams see what was checked, and how the spacecraft behaved under those checks.
nasa-tm-19680023742-a-technique-for-long:
A July 1968 Goddard preprint, X-643-68-275, presents a technique for long arc fitting. The test case is the orbit of IMP 3, also called Explorer 28. Orbit fitters usually work with short arcs, brief spans of tracking data. The study asks whether one solution can stay consistent across a far longer stretch of the satellite's travel.

The author obtained a single arc spanning one hundred twenty orbits of the highly stretched IMP 3 path. That long arc predicted perigee passage within one minute of the short arc answers, across a very long orbital period. The report concludes that such eccentric orbits, barely touched by air drag, suit accurate long term orbit studies well.
nasa-tm-19690013543-direct-measurements-:
P. L. Dyson wrote this February 1969 Goddard preprint, numbered X-621-69-57, on irregularities in the topside ionosphere. Langmuir probe data from Alouette II, gathered over three months in fall 1966, are examined directly. The topside ionosphere is not smooth: its electron density carries fine bumps that can disturb radio signals crossing the region.

Dyson finds the bumps gather in patches hundreds of kilometers wide. Single irregularities run less than two kilometers along the satellite path, with strengths from the detection limit up to seventy percent. They appear more often at night than by day, the abstract notes. Separate chapters compare this fine structure with the better known spread F condition, then interpret both.
specimens-with-memoirs-of-the-less-known:
Rev. George Gilfillan edits Specimens with Memoirs of the Less-Known British Poets. A first essay of his own opens the set. This is the complete Volume I. Its date reads M.DCCC.LX, that is, 1860. The essay treats English poetry's origin and growth. It runs up to Chaucer and Gower. Many call Chaucer the father of English poetry. Gilfillan holds that a dawn went before that sun. To reflect that dawn is his aim here.

Britain under Rome stayed rough and little lettered, he argues. No great Latin halls stand in the island. No British-born writer ranks among Latin verse masters. Latin never drove out the old Gaelic speech here. In the fifth century a German speech came in. Men call that speech Anglo-Saxon. The British tongue drew back before it. Proud as a lion, it held the mountain fastnesses of Wales.
the-circassian-slave-or-the-sultan-s-fav:
Maturin Murray Ballou stands behind this second record of the same 1851 Boston novelette, whose title page credits only Lieutenant Murray. Its front matter matches the other record: the same publisher's note, the same contents, and the same preface. The tale is set in Constantinople and the Caucasus, in quite modern times.

The publisher first ran the story in the Pictorial Drawing Room Companion and presents it as a specimen of that journal's entertaining tales. The preface points to the lands bordering the Black Sea, the Sea of Marmora, and the Bosphorus. Contents chapters run from the slave market and the sultan's harem to a slave ship, an elopement, an escape from the harem, and a chase. Since both records carry identical front matter, readers should treat them as two listings of one work, not as two distinct tales.
the-kipling-reader-selections-from-the-b: Macmillan's school reader gathers selections from Rudyard Kipling. This copy is the new and revised edition of 1923. A first edition came in 1900. Reprintings followed in nearly every year since. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The selections themselves do not appear. The prose runs from Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and Wee Willie Winkie onward. Mowgli's Brothers, Tiger Tiger, and The Lost Legion appear. A Germ-Destroyer and Tods' Amendment follow. The poetry opens with The Native Born and The Flowers. The English Flag closes the list shown.
the-vicomte-de-bragelonne-or-ten-years-l: Alexandre Dumas's Vicomte de Bragelonne, or Ten Years Later, completes The Three Musketeers and Twenty Years After. The pages present here are title pages only, so the novel's text does not appear. They identify this copy as part two, volume four of a set described as complete in nine volumes, published by Peter Fenelon Collier in New York in 1893. An illustration caption shows a king beginning to climb a ladder that has just been placed. The edition boasts copious engravings by eminent French and American artists.
